Among all surveyed payers, 71% anticipated adopting an ISP strategy in the next 12 months and would adjust rebates accordingly. These payers plan to track diagnosis through prior authorization (54%) or through physicians documenting diagnosis separately (42%). To determine the value of a drug in a specific indication, payers will most commonly rely upon randomized clinical trial data with 52% citing phase II/III or postâ€approval research as the most important resource. Another 28% cited realâ€world data or evidence as the most important resource, while the remaining 20% will leverage other clinical information, clinical guidelines, or thirdâ€party value assessment tools. Conclusions: Survey responses point to ISP use expanding, fueled by cost concerns and improved ability to patients and measure clinical effectiveness. The overwhelming reliance on clinical trial data to determine clinical value suggest that that payers prefer to leverage the existing tools historically used in value assessment. However, the 49% that cited RWE as either the most or secondâ€most important resource point to RWEâ€™s growing importance in ISP as payers become more comfortable with leveraging the dataâ€™s potential.

Introduction: Health care spending rose from 5% to 17.8% of GDP between 1960 and 2015. Clinicians and researchers must engage in increasing health care value â€ better outcomes at less cost. Personalized screening is one such opportunity. The Patient Centered Outcomes Research Institute recently funded WISDOM (Women Informed to Screen Depending On Measures of risk), a randomized trial to tests the safety and efficacy of basing starting age, stopping age, frequency and modality of breast cancer screening on individual risk (Clinical Trials Identifier NCT02620852). The personalized arm of WISDOM integrates genetic testing into the risk algorithm. Funding for the clinical services of WISDOM (genetic test, risk assessment, highâ€risk counseling) are expected to be covered (health plans, insurers). Risk determines the frequency, time to initiate screening and drives cost of downstream screening services. The cost of genetic testing is now less than $250, comparable to a mammogram. The WISDOM study model brings payers, policy makers, provider, technology, and advocate partners together to generate evidence to see if risk based screening is as safe, less morbid, preferred by women, promotes prevention, and has greater health care value. Health plans need to know the value proposition, thus we evaluated financial implications of coverage for riskâ€based screening. Methods: A model was developed to compare costs and benefits of riskâ€based vs. current screening practices from the perspective of a health plan. Modeled cohorts resembled a screening population with risk determining screening interval for the riskâ€based model, and average time between mammograms determining the interval for the model of current screening practices. Model parameters were gathered from published literature, national databases, early findings from WISDOM and health plan claims data. Sensitivity analysis was performed on all parameters, including costs of clinical services, screening rates, and health plan turnover. The clinical services specific to WISDOM use a fixedâ€fee schedule, and not varied in the model. All other costs were conservative, based on Medicare rates and published literature. Results: We estimated that over five years, riskâ€based screening is at worst cost neutral with potential for savings of up to $215 per participant. Based on current trial enrollment, we estimated that 30 per 1,000 health plan enrollees would join, resulting in an upfront cost of $6,000 for WISDOMâ€specific services, primarily the genetic test, and $600 in ongoing costs after Year 1. However, the health plan would save on mammogram and work up costs as participants would receive an average of 2â€3 fewer mammograms over five years. Savings are sensitive to the age of participants, cost of mammograms, and savings increase over time. Per participant, fiveâ€year savings of $300 and $35 for those aged 40â€49 and 65â€74 respectively, and increased costs of $30 for those aged 50â€64. Overall, an upfront investment of $6,000 per 1,000 health plan enrollees (30 participants) yields $3,800 in fiveâ€year savings. Conclusion: Personalized screening could provide cost savings and has the potential to increase health care value. Enrollment in the Wisdom study is ongoing and results will be reported in 5 years.

Background: P4P programs are expanding nationally despite mixed evidence. With Advocate Health System (Chicago, IL) we conducted a hybrid prospective randomized and quasiâ€experimental trial assessing whether increasing bonus sizes or the behavioral economics principles loss aversion and social pressure could improve P4P's effectiveness. This is the first randomized trial to test behavioral economic principles in P4P. Methods: The design was a quasiâ€experimental comparison involving patients treated by physicians in the Trinity Organization versus Nonâ€Trinity physicians at Advocate. Nonâ€Trinity physicians were matched based on preâ€intervention (2015) performance level and 2014â€2015 historic trend. The patients were clusterâ€randomized by attributed physician to 3 arms: 1) An active control with a larger bonus size of $ 3,333 or 10% increase (666 patients and 9 physicians); 2) The larger bonus size with loss aversion by preâ€funding incentives in a health system bank account in the physician's name (1,506 patients and 13 physicians); and 3) The larger bonus size with social pressure by making the performance bonus determined by individual (50%) and group (50%) performance (1,358 patients and 13 physicians). Using a differenceâ€inâ€differences design, we compared changes at Trinity as a whole (an increase in bonus size) to propensityâ€matched nonâ€Trinity physicians with physician fixedâ€effects and patient riskâ€adjustment. The primary outcome variable was the proportion of evidenceâ€based quality measures met for patients with chronic conditions. Results: The Trinity RCT included 3,530 patients randomized via 35 physicians and the nonâ€Trinity matched cohort included 3,801 patients across 35 physicians. There were no differences across physician characteristics. Trinity patients were more likely to be black (68% vs. 17%; P< 0.001) and younger (64 vs. 66 years; P< 0.001). There were small differences in patient characteristics by Arm. Arm 2 had the highest average number of chronic conditions (Arm 1, 1.54 conditions; Arm 2, 1.63 conditions; Arm 3, 1.60 conditions; P< 0.001) and greatest proportion of black patients (Arm 1, 64%; Arm 2, 59%; Arm 3, 80%; P< 0.001). In both unadjusted and adjusted analysis, Trinity patients received a larger increase in evidenceâ€based care relative to nonâ€Trinity patients from 2015 to 2016 (Adjusted resultsâ€Trinity 86.49% to 90.70% vs. Nonâ€Trinity 87.50% to 89.27%; differenceâ€inâ€difference 2.4%; P< 0.001). The RCT within Trinity did not reveal significant additional improvement between Arm 2 (larger bonus + loss aversion) and Arm 3 (larger bonus + enhanced social pressure) versus a larger bonus only (Arm 1) (P=0.52). Conclusions: Inthe first RCTcomparing behavioral economic principles and increasing bonuses in P4P, an increase in bonus size resulted in significantly improved quality for chronic care patients relative to a comparison group. Adding loss aversion and enhanced social pressure did not lead to further quality improvement.

Objectives: While CARâ€T therapies are considered breakthrough therapies, they have experienced low uptake in realâ€world practice, due to challenges related to efficacy, patient accessibility, and cost. This research explored the current CARâ€T utilization and reimbursement challenges as well as introduction of innovative payment systems being piloted. Methods: Data from a realâ€world patient record database (Global Oncology MonitorÂ©), from 1/2018 to 10/2018 on eligible US patients (N=616) was included. Physicians randomly selected patients diagnosed with diffuse large Bâ€cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and currently on an antiâ€cancer regimen, reported on their practices related to CARâ€T use. Analysis of CMS reimbursement and various payment models was performed through secondary research. Primary research was also conducted via qualitative interviews with US payers (N=5). Results: Utilization of CARâ€Ts in areas such as DLBCL remains low (âˆ¼2%), due to reasons such as financial burden/lack of insurance and accessibility issues. US payers debate whether CARâ€T treatment should occur in the inpatient setting, placing greater financial burden on hospitals/providers vs. in the outpatient setting, shifting the cost burden onto the patient. CMSâ€™ current inpatient payment policy for CARâ€Ts entails a DRG base payment of $39,000 and NTAP maximum of $186,500, which does not cover the total cost of care for either the therapy or hospitalization. Commercial payers are also struggling with an optimal coverage solution that will ensure access to a potentially lifeâ€saving treatment. Payers reference innovative payment models such as installment plans and outcomesâ€based agreements viable for CARâ€T therapies. For example, a stateâ€wide initiative in Massachusetts piloting a payment installment plan for a novel gene therapy, where payment is spread out over four years, could be leveraged for CARâ€T therapies. Conclusions: As the CARâ€T landscape evolves, it will be critical to continue to engage with payers and providers to identify solutions to address the financial toxicity, maximize patient access and improve uptake.

Purpose/Objective(s): Third party administrators often cite overutilization and cost as justifications for restrictive proton beam therapy (PBT) coverage policies. We collaborated with a stateâ€wide selfâ€funded employer, The University of Texas System (UTS), to implement a PBT coverage pilot ensuring appropriate access to care without increasing cost. This pilot conducts a valueâ€based assessment of PBT through evaluation of utilization trends and comprehensive charge analysis of medical claims. Materials/Methods: UTS adopted our institutionâ€™s evidenceâ€based treatment guidelines and inclusion criteria which expanded PBT coverage by 5 additional body sites: head and neck (HN), esophagus, breast, thoracic, and prostate (GU). Coverage also included patients on 1 of any 6 NCI/NIH randomized controlled trials. The pilot obtained IRB approval, with all patients enrolled on a prospective research trial. The majority of patients with UTS benefits treated with PBT during this time were approved via the pilot. Patient satisfaction (PROs), safety (grade 4â€5 complications), treatment related toxicities, and total billed charges (cost of care) were pilot metrics. The primary endpoint was cost of care, including all claims 1 month preâ€treatment, through the PBT course, up to 6 months postâ€treatment. PBT claims were compared with caseâ€matched (by employer, site, indication, and stage) photon patients who were treated within the same enrollment period. Results: Enrollment initiated April 2016, accruing 32 patients over 3 years, vs. predicted utilization of 120 patients (p<.01). The average pilot prior authorization time was <1 business day, vs. the historical preâ€pilot average of 17 business days. Of the 32 pilot patients, 22 (9 HN, 8 GU, 3 breast, 2 thoracic) were treated with PBT with a median followâ€up of 20.1 months. There were no Grade 4â€5 toxicities. During this timeframe, 25 patients who met pilot eligibility were instead treated with photons. Out of these, 17 were caseâ€matched to 17 PBT pilot patients with â‰¥6 month followâ€up. Median number of fractions was 30 for both groups (p=.96). On analysis, employer costs with PBT were dramatically lower than estimated (initially expecting an increase for PBT), with average billed charges actually 4.4% lower for PBT (p=.84). Percentage of RT charges to total charges was 77% vs. 64% for PBT and photons (p=.09), respectively, with higher ancillary care utilization by the latter. Conclusion: This stateâ€wide insurance coverage pilot demonstrates that appropriate access to PBT does not result in overutilization or increased employer cost. Objective evidenceâ€based treatment guidelines and policies can ensure appropriate patient selection while reducing administrative burden. Collaboration among employers, payers, and providers can improve access to PBT without increasing cost.

Background: Greater orientation toward primary care has been associated with better quality and lower costs of care. Health systems are growing in the United States and increasingly shape care delivery. In this study, we explore variation in primary care spending as a proportion of total spending among Medicare feeâ€forâ€service beneficiaries who seek care from health systemâ€affiliated provider organizations (POs) versus unaffiliated POs, as well as across health systems. Methods: Using 100% 2015 Medicare claims, enrollment, and provider data, we attributed 6,602,562 beneficiaries to 10,863 health system POs and 9,902,449 beneficiaries to nonâ€health system 88,600 POs, attributing beneficiaries to POs (identified by TIN) responsible for at least 30% of their evaluation and management service and identifying systemâ€affiliated POs using the SK& A provider database. We then assessed the percentage of their total medical and prescription drug spending on primary care. We defined primary care spending according to narrow and broad definitions of primary care providers (PCPS) and services. The narrow PCP definition included Family Practice, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, and General Practice. The broad definition also included Nurse Practitioners, Physician Assistants, Geriatric Medicine, and Gynecology. Both excluded hospitalists. The narrow services definition included evaluation and management visits, preventive visits, care transition or coordination services, and inâ€office preventive services, screening, and counseling. The broad definition included all professional services billed by PCPS. Results: Beneficiaries attributed to health system POs had less spending on primary care than those attributed to nonâ€health system POs (e.g., 2.5% versus 3.3% for the narrow PCP and service definition). Among health systems, the primary care spending percentage varied according to the definition used (from 2.5% of total spending for the narrow PCP and service definition to 6.0% for the broad definitions), did not vary with the number of physicians in a system, and increased with the percentage of system physicians who were PCPS (ranging from 1.7% of spending for systems with less than 25% PCPS to 3.3% for systems with at least 75% PCPS, for the narrow PCP and service definition). Conclusions: Compared to health system POs, nonâ€health system POs have lower proportions of total spending on primary care. Health systems with greater primary care specialty composition have higher proportion of medical spending on primary care. As state policymakers working to establish minimum thresholds for the proportion of health care spending on primary care can be informed by information about the variation in primary care spending among health systems. Describing the proportion of spending devoted to primary care among POs can enable future research examining the relationship between primary care spending and the quality and efficiency of care.

Background: The value of health spending depends on the public's willingness to pay higher taxes or reduce nonâ€health program expenditures. Heterogeneity in preferences for taxes and programs raises questions about how to identify policyâ€relevant healthâ€expenditure values. Healthpolicy questions also may require larger samples than commonly found in the discreteâ€choice experiment (DCE) health literature to inform prioritysetting decisions. Objective: To apply latentâ€class analysis using a very large data set to account for a large number of locationâ€specific preference correlates. Methods: 10,000 US adults completed an online DCE survey. Respondents answered 5 3â€alternative tradeâ€off questions consisting of status quo and two budget alternatives. Each budget profile included a mentalâ€health program plus 2 programs randomly selected for each respondent from 4 programs: Food safety, disaster relief, unemployment, and motorâ€vehicle safety. Benefits were scaled proportional to state population sizes. Modeling included splitâ€sample, conditional and randomâ€parameters logit, and various latentâ€class specifications, including predetermined and unconditional class assignments, with and without random parameters, with and without scale adjustments, with and without covariates, and with and without attributeâ€covariate interactions. Results: Aggregate, splitâ€sample, and latentâ€class analysis with predeterminedâ€classes by state size yielded highly significant, but disordered, effectâ€coded coefficients and implausible value estimates. Unconditional latentâ€class models explained the implausible aggregate estimates as the result of averaging highly heterogenous group preferences. Plausible latent classes included groups who rejected taxation for any purpose (21% of the sample), who approved taxation for any purpose (14%), who had welldefined priorities among programs and were: Highly sensitive to (24%), ignored (21%), or less sensitive to tax increases (20%). Only the latter group passed a scope test on tax levels. Conclusions: A rare opportunity to analyze a very large DCE dataset offered numerous options for wellâ€powered hypothesis tests but also presented challenges in how to interpret and aggregate dissimilar preferences to support decision making.

Research Objective: Through the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) Model, mandatory bundled payments for lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR) have produced 3â€4% episode cost savings with stable quality. Though CJR targets Medicare feeâ€forâ€service patients, it may prompt broad care delivery changes that â€œspill overâ€ to other, nonâ€Medicare feeâ€forâ€service patients. Prior work demonstrating spillovers in CJR only evaluated utilization outcomes among a subset of hospitals, thereby compromising the program's randomized design and failing to evaluate programâ€wide utilization and spending spillovers. Therefore, we used more comprehensive data and an approach that preserved CJR's randomized design to examine the impact of program participation on spillovers for commercially insured and Medicare Advantage patients. Study Design: We used 2011â€2017 claims data from the Health Care Cost Institute (full claims of 25% of all insured US individuals younger than 65) to construct LEJR episodes for commercially insured and Medicare Advantage patients, and data from Medicare to identify markets (CJR markets) mandated to participate in CJR from April 2016 to December 2017. Leveraging the marketâ€level randomized design of CJR, we used hierarchical multivariable generalized linear modelsâ€adjusted for patient and market factors and incorporating time fixed effects and hospital and market random effectsâ€to evaluate changes in LEJR episode spending, discharge to institutional postacute care, and quality outcomes (LEJR complication rate, readmissions, emergency department visits) in CJR versus nonâ€CJR markets. Additionally, we conducted stratified analyses by evaluating the association between CJR participation and outcomes for Medicare Advantage patients and commercially insured patients separately. To evaluate the robustness of our findings, we conducted sensitivity analyses that incorporated low volume CJR hospitals, hospital factors, and LEJR episodes with low index hospitalization spending. Statistical tests were 2â€tailed and significant at Î±=0.05. Population Studied: 418 016 Medicare Advantage or commercially insured patients receiving LEJR in 75 CJR or 121 nonâ€CJR markets Principal Findings: There were small differences in patient characteristics, including prior health care utilization, between CJR and nonâ€CJR markets. In adjusted analysis, patients who underwent joint replacement in CJR and nonâ€CJR markets did not differ with respect to episode spending (difference of â€$157, 95% CI â€$1,043 to $728, P = .73) or probability of discharge to institutional postacute care (difference of â€1.1%, 95% CI â€3.2% to 1.0 %, P = .31). Patients in CJR and nonâ€CJR markets also did not differ with respect to changes in quality outcomes. Stratified and sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings. Conclusions: There was a lack of evidence supporting spillovers from CJR to patients insured through private health plans. Implications for Policy or Practice: Unlike voluntary programs, for which spillovers have been demonstrated, mandatory reforms may fail to create strong enough incentives for participants to enact broad care redesign and generate spillovers. Additionally, alternatives to the marketâ€level randomization used in CJR may be needed to address smaller sample sizes and increase the ability to detect meaningful spillovers. Both issues pose notable implications as policy makers consider whether and how to implement mandatory versus voluntary reforms in the future. Finally, this analysis also underscores the need to go beyond subgroup analyses and conduct programâ€wide spillover evaluations, which generate the most policyâ€and practiceâ€relevant results..

BACKGROUND: As a strategy to improve health care value for joint replacement surgery, mandatory bundled payments have produced 3â€4% in episode cost savings with stable quality in the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) Model. Though CJR targets Medicare feeâ€forservice patients, it may prompt broad organizational care delivery changes that â€œspill overâ€ to other patients, such as those insured through private health plans. However, previous literature reporting evidence of spillovers has only used data on a subset of hospitals, thereby potentially compromising the randomized study design of CJR. We addressed these limitations in examining the impact of CJR participation on quality, utilization, and spending outcomes for commercially insured and Medicare Advantage (MA) patients. METHODS: Our analysis used 2011â€2016 Health Care Cost Institute claims encompassing 418,016 MA or commercially insured patients who underwent lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR) surgery at hospitals in 75 CJR markets and 121 nonâ€CJR markets across the US. We leveraged the randomized design of CJR at the marketâ€level to evaluate changes in LEJR outcomes among CJR hospitals, compared to changes at nonâ€ CJR hospitals. Primary outcomes were changes in 90â€day total LEJR episode spending and discharge to institutional postâ€acute care. Additional quality outcomes included the LEJR complication rate, 90â€day readmissions rate, and emergency department visit rate. All models were adjusted for patient and marketâ€ level factors, and incorporated time fixedâ€effects and hospital and market random effects. RESULTS: Patient characteristics, including prior health care utilization, varied between CJR and nonâ€CJR markets, though they were not clinically meaningful. In adjusted analysis, patients who underwent LEJR surgery in CJR and nonâ€CJR markets did not differ with respect to episode spending (difference of â€$157, 95% CI â€$1,043 to $728, p=0.73) or probability of discharge to institutional postâ€acute care (difference of â€1.1%, 95% CI â€3.2% to 1.0 %, p=0.31). Patients in CJR and nonâ€CJR markets also did not differ with respect to changes in other quality outcomes. Stratified and sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings. CONCLUSIONS: In contrast to findings from previous literature, there was a lack of evidence of programâ€ wide CJR spillovers to patients insured through private health plans. Mandatory payment reforms may have limits in their effects. (Figure Presented).

Research Objective: In 2017, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services launched the Million HeartsÂ® Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) Risk Reduction Model with the aim to reduce firstâ€time heart attacks and strokes among highâ€risk Medicare feeâ€forâ€ services (FFS) beneficiaries within 5 years. This largeâ€scale randomized trial pays providers to assess each of their Medicare patient's risk of a heart attack or stroke and then makes additional payment if they reduce CVD risk among their highâ€risk cohort. We assess whether, during its first two years, the model increased use of CVD medications, reduced incidence of heart attacks and strokes, and reduced Medicare spending. Study Design: A pragmatic, clusterâ€randomized trial. CMS enrolled 516 organizations (primary and specialty practices, health centers, and hospitals) throughout the country and assigned half to the intervention group. For the 313 organizations that enrolled beneficiaries in 2017, we linked enrollment and clinical data with Medicare claims and estimated impacts as interventionâ€control differences (regression adjusted) in outcomes. Population Studied: 300 550 Medicare FFS beneficiaries, 18% of whom were high risk (â‰¥30% or higher risk of a heart attack or stroke in the next 10 years) and 40% were medium risk (15%â€30% risk) in both groups. Intervention and control group beneficiaries were similar at enrollment in demographics, CVD risk factors, and recent utilization and spending. Principal Findings: Among the highâ€risk group, almost 40% of CVD risk at baseline was modifiable, mainly from elevated blood pressure and cholesterol. Highâ€risk intervention group enrollees were 4 percentage points more likely than the control group (28 vs 24%, P < .001) to initiate or intensify statins or antihypertensive medications factors within 6 months of enrollment. When including the larger mediumâ€risk groupâ€for whom CMS does not separately pay for CVD risk reductionâ€rates of initiation or intensification were 3 percentage points higher in the intervention versus control groups (23% vs 20%, P < .001). Over a mean followâ€up of 17 months, the incidence of firstâ€time heart attack and stroke was similar in the intervention versus the control groups for the highâ€risk group (90% confidence interval for hazard ratio: 0.93â€1.14) and for the mediumâ€and highâ€risk groups combined (90% CI: 0.93, 1.06). Medicare Part A and B spending was also similar in the intervention and control groups. Conclusions: Thus far, the Million Hearts model has improved initiation and intensification of medications to treat modifiable risk factors among the highâ€risk group, with positive spillover to the much larger mediumâ€risk group. However, the model has not reduced heart attacks and strokes or generated any savings to offset model costs. Implications for Policy or Practice: While CVD risk factors have declined substantially over the past 50 years, progress has slowed recently and even reversed in some groups. Valueâ€based purchasing efforts to date have focused on achieving control for individual CVD risk factors. This trial shows that a new â€œpay for preventionâ€ approach that rewards assessing and reducing total CVD risk (combining individual risk factors into a single score readily interpretable by patients and providers) can improve use of CVD medications. More time is needed to assess whether the model will eventually reduce incidence of heart attacks and strokes..

Objectives: To compare changes in adherence and outâ€ofâ€pocket costs among patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) before and after stateâ€level oral oncolytic parity laws, which require that oral oncolytics under the pharmacy benefit are covered similarly to parenteral oncolytics under the medical benefit. Methods: Adults with CML, â‰¥1 pharmacy claim for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) and residence in any of 41 states that implemented oral oncolytic parity legislation between 1â€1â€2007 and 12â€31â€2017 were identified from the IBMÂ® MarketScanÂ® Commercial Claims Database. Continuous enrollment 3 months before and 6 months after the first TKI claim date (index date) was required. The proportion of days covered (PDC) was calculated and 30â€day outâ€ofâ€pocket costs (copayments, coinsurance, and deductibles as 2017 United States dollars) were assessed in the 6 months postâ€index; patients with a PDC â‰¥0.85 were categorized as adherent. Differences in outcomes before and after parity were evaluated, controlling for membership in health plans subject to parity (fullyâ€insured health plans [FIHPs]) or not (selfâ€funded health plans [SFHPs]). Results: Of 1,887 CML patients initiating a TKI, 678 (35.9%) were members of FIHPs and 1,209 (64.1%) of SFHPs. After parity, mean PDC improved in FIHPs and SFHPs (0.85 to 0.87 and 0.87 to 0.90, respectively). TKI adherence improved from 69.2% to 73.2% of patients in FIHPs (P=0.2817) and similarly from 73.6% to 78.3% in SFHPs (P=0.0585). In FIHPs, median (Q1â€“Q3) outâ€ofâ€pocket costs perâ€patient increased from $33.48 ($18.12â€“$63.41) to $37.78 ($5.35â€“$112.03), while in SFHPs they increased from $38.26 ($23.69â€“$85.27) to $52.84 ($19.05â€“$112.03). Conclusions: Oral oncolytic parity legislation has produced minimal impact on TKI adherence and outâ€ofâ€pocket costs among CML patients. To improve clinical outcomes and protect patients from rising outâ€ofâ€pocket costs, policymakers may consider amending current legislation.

Objectives: Interest in value frameworks that account for values other than narrowly defined healthâ€state utilities offers opportunities to apply established statedâ€preference methods to quantify community benefits of stateâ€sponsored mentalâ€health programs, including reduced homelessness, unemployment, and criminality. The aim of this study was to quantify the publicâ€™s perceived value for publicly funded programs to treat severe mental illness. Methods: A national sample of 10,000 US adults completed an online discreteâ€choice experiment survey. Respondents answered five 3â€alternative tradeâ€off questions consisting of status quo (no increased spending) and 2 budgetâ€increase alternatives. Each budget profile included expanding a mentalâ€health program plus 2 respondentâ€specific expansions randomly selected from 4 nonâ€health programs. Statistical modeling accounted for latentâ€class preference heterogeneity, state size, region, and individualâ€specific covariates. Results: We omitted from the analysis 23% of the sample who rejected any increase in taxes for any purpose. Depending on state size and region, latent classes for the remainder of the sample included groups of participants who had wellâ€defined priorities for mentalâ€health programs and were relatively sensitive (32%â€42%) or insensitive (21% to 35%) to increased taxes. Other groups ignored tax increases (21%â€23%) or provided incoherent preference data (12%â€18%). We imputed zero willingness to pay additional taxes for the latter two classes and for tax objectors. For a mentalâ€health program expansion that would treat an additional 1500 patients in mediumâ€sized states in the Northeast, Midwest, South, and West regions of the US, the median acceptable increase in annual taxes was $218 (209, 227), $429 (415, 442), $252 (242, 263), and $216 (140, 293), respectively. Conclusions: Focusing narrowly on direct health outcomes understates the value of benefits to patients, their families, and communities of successfully treating severe mental illness. Even after accounting for a significant proportion of generalâ€population respondents who indicated zero perceived benefits for improved mentalâ€health treatment, we obtained significant values for total community benefits.

BACKGROUND: Bundled payments have garnered widespread participation from physician group practices (PGPs) and hospitals. However, while hospital participation has been wellâ€studied and shown to achieve savings with stable quality, there are no peerâ€reviewed studies assessing PGP participation. This knowledge gap is notable given that PGP participation in other payment models, such as accountable care organizations, has been associated with stronger effects than hospital participation. Therefore, we compared PGP and hospital BPCI participation and their relationship with episode outcomes. METHODS: We used 2010â€2017 Medicare claims and generalized linear models to conduct a difference inâ€differences analysis of patients receiving care under BPCI via propensityâ€matched BPCI vs Nonâ€BPCI physicians and BPCI vs Nonâ€BPCI hospitals for the 10 highest volume episodes (5 surgical, 5 medical). This quasiâ€experimental analysis mirrored a 2x2 factorial randomized trial in which patients received care from either PGPs in BPCI, Hospitals in BPCI, both (i.e., receiving care at BPCI hospitals from BPCI PGP physicians), or neither. The primary outcome was 90â€day total episode spending. Secondary outcomes were 90â€day readmissions and 90â€day mortality. We confirmed parallel trends in the preâ€BPCI time period. RESULTS: The matched sample included 600,803 patients receiving care from 2,582 physicians in BPCI PGPs, 644,627 patients receiving care from 384 BPCI Hospitals, 74,858 patients receiving care from both BPCI PGPs and Hospitals, and 1,268,933 patients receiving care outside of BPCI (SMD<0.1 for all PGP and hospital characteristics). Compared to patients receiving care outside of BPCI, episode spending was differentially lower for those receiving care under BPCI PGPs (adjusted differenceâ€inâ€ differences [aDID] â€$520, 95% CI â€$615 to â€$424, p<0.001) and hospitals (aDID â€$1073, 95% CI â€$1164 to â€$982, p<0.001). Savings were larger for BPCI Hospitals than PGPs (p <0.001) and receiving care under both PGPs and Hospitals was not associated with additional differential changes in episode spending (aDID $225, 95% CI â€$29 to $479, p=0.08). Compared to patients receiving care outside of BPCI, mortality was differentially lower for patients receiving care from BPCI PGPs (aDID â€0.6%, 95% CI â€0.7% to â€0.4%, p<0.001) and BPCI Hospitals (aDID â€0.6%, 95% CI â€0.8% to â€0.5%, p<0.001). Readmissions were differentially lower among patients cared for by BPCI Hospitals but not those cared for by BPCI PGPs. CONCLUSIONS: PGP participation in bundled payments was associated with episode savings and lower mortality. Savings were smaller than hospitalâ€associated savings, while mortality was comparable. Unlike in other payment models, hospitals may have advantages compared to PGPs in bundled payments. LEARNING OBJECTIVE #1: List comparative effects of physician versus hospital participation in bundled payments LEARNING OBJECTIVE #2: Describe advantages of participating hospitals over physicians.

Introduction: The FDA approved ramucirumab (RAM) in combination with erlotinib (ERL) in 2020 for firstâ€line treatment of metastatic nonâ€small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) exon 19 deletions or exon 21 (L858R) mutations. The RELAY phase III trial (NCT02411448) showed a statistically significant improvement in progressionâ€free survival (19.4 months [RAM+ERL] versus 12.4 months [placebo+ERL] p<0.0001). The objective of this analysis was to estimate the budgetary impact (BI) of introducing RAM+ERL as firstâ€line treatment of metastatic EGFRâ€mutated NSCLC using the U.S. Commercial payer and Medicare perspectives. Methods: The BI model estimated the costs of metastatic EGFRâ€mutated NSCLC, before and after adoption of RAM+ERL in a hypothetical cohort over a 5â€year time horizon. Eligible patient population was estimated using U.S. epidemiology data. Clinical data were obtained from randomized clinical trials and U.S. prescribing information, and cost data were obtained from online sources and published literature. Market share (MS) projections were based on market research data. Annual costs were estimated along with perâ€memberâ€perâ€month (PMPM) costs in 2020 U.S. dollars. Of 1,000,000 hypothetical Commercial healthâ€plan members, 10 patients were eligible for treatment with RAM+ERL (193 from Medicare). Sensitivity analyses (SA) assessed the effect of model parameters on results. Results: Overall, 1.50% cost increase was predicted from a total budget of $13,200,820 (Table) with annual cost increases ranging from 1.21%â€1.72% over the 5â€year period. BI of PMPM cost was estimated to be <source.003â€<source.004, and drug acquisition cost was the dominating contributor to the budget with 89.0% ($11,886,858). Results were similar for the Medicare population. The BIM predicted that RAM+ERL would gain 5.3% ($143,490) of the U.S. Commercial market when it becomes available in Year 1 and increase to 9.2% ($245,982) in Year 5. In the Commercial perspective, 77.9% of the drug costs were predicted to come from osimertinib followed by 6.3% from afatinib and 6.6% from other treatments in Year 5. Based on oneâ€way SA, the budget was most sensitive to changes in acquisition costs for RAM, osimertinib and patient body weight. When MS for RAM+ERL was assumed to increase by 30% from the base case, the overall BI reduced from 1.50% to 0.72% as RAM+ERL partially replaced regimens such as osimertinib, which has higher treatment costs. [Formula presented] Conclusion: This analysis predicted a modest U.S. health plan BI of adopting RAM+ERL for firstâ€line treatment of metastatic EGFRâ€mutated NSCLC. Primary drivers of the BI included drug acquisition cost and forecasted MS. Keywords: budget impact, ramucirumab plus erlotinib, EGFR+ NSCLC

BACKGROUND: For patients that face barriers to filling their prescriptions, the availability of medication access services at their site of care can mean the difference between receiving prescribed drug therapy, and undue interruptions in care. Hospitals often provide medication access services that are not reimbursed by payers; however, they can be challenging to sustain. The 340B Drug Pricing Program allows covered entities to generate savings through discounted pricing for certain outpatient medications, which can then be used to provide more comprehensive services, including medication access services. OBJECTIVE: To characterize medication access services provided at hospitals that participate in the 340B Drug Pricing Program compared to hospitals that do not participate in the 340B Program. METHODS: Primary questionnaire response data was collected from a national sample of Directors of Pharmacy at nonâ€federal acute care hospitals from March 2019 to May 2019. American Hospital Association Data Viewer was used to collect demographic information on 1,531 hospitals. Hospitals were excluded if they had 199 beds or fewer, did not have a unique Medicare provider ID, were federally owned, were located outside the continental U.S., or were nonâ€acute care hospitals that served niche patient populations. This study utilized a proportional stratified sampling strategy to administer an electronic questionnaire to 340B and nonâ€340B hospitals to assess the number and type of medication access service offerings. A final randomized sample of 500 hospitals were administered the questionnaire, and data was collected through recorded responses in Qualtrics software. RESULTS: 340B hospitals provided a significantly higher average number of medication access services compared to nonâ€340B hospitals (6.20 vs. 3.91, p = 0.0001), adjusted for differences in hospital size and ownership type. For all nine medication access services that were assessed, a higher percentage of 340B hospitals reported providing the service compared to nonâ€340B hospitals. This difference was statistically significant for six out of nine programs assessed. CONCLUSIONS: 340B hospitals provided more medication access services, on average, than comparably sized nonâ€340B hospitals, suggesting that hospitals participating in the 340B Drug Pricing Program may be better positioned to create and administer programs that support medication access services.

Objectives: 1. Identify patientâ€level barriers to hospice access. 2. Describe financial constraints faced by hospice organizations that may result in inequitable access to hospice care. Background: Many hospices have enrollment policies that restrict access for patients with diseases that require expensive treatments and have less predictable trajectories. Patients with two such diseases, heart failure (HF) and cystic fibrosis (CF), may experience inequities in endâ€ofâ€life care; yet, no research exists regarding the specific patientâ€level factors that drive hospice agency decisionâ€making. Research Objectives: To investigate if medication cost, complexity of disease, and/or diagnosis is associated with hospice willingness to accept patients. Methods: Online survey consisting of six patient profiles: â€œhighâ€cost, highâ€complexity,â€ â€œlowâ€cost, highâ€complexity,â€ and â€œlowâ€cost, lowâ€complexityâ€ for both HF and CF. Each profile included demographics, medical history, prognosis, goals of care, and medications with costs. Individuals involved in hospice decisions (recruited via AAHPM, HPNA, NHPCO listservs, and Twitter advertising) were randomized to view one profile and asked the likelihood of accepting that patient to hospice at their organization, along with questions regarding barriers. Bivariate tests were used to determine associations between various demographic, clinical, and organizational factors and likelihood of acceptance. Results: N=502. The likelihoods of acceptance in CF were: 79.8% (highâ€cost, highâ€complexity, n=77), 92.3% (lowâ€cost, highâ€complexity, n=77), and 91.6% (lowâ€cost, lowâ€complexity, n=85). The likelihoods of acceptance in HF were: 65.6% (highâ€cost, highâ€complexity, n=78), 87.4% (lowâ€cost, highâ€complexity, n=90), and 96.7% (lowâ€cost, lowâ€complexity, n=87). For both HF and CF, respondents were less likely to accept the highâ€cost, highâ€complexity patient than the lowâ€cost, highâ€complexity patient (both p<0.001). For HF, respondents were significantly less likely to accept the lowâ€cost, highâ€complexity patient than the lowâ€cost, lowâ€complexity patient (p=0.004); for CF, there was no significant difference between the likelihood to accept the two lowâ€cost patients. Treatment cost was the most common barrier to acceptance for four of the six patient profiles. Conclusion: Patients receiving expensive and/or complex treatments for palliation may have difficulty accessing hospice care. Implications for Research, Policy, or Practice: Hospice policies should be reevaluated to ensure equitable access, while balancing financial constraints of providing endâ€ofâ€life care.

Background: Response to public health emergencies often requires a cadre of healthcare providers who have received specialized training. An open question is how to efficiently recruit and train providers in a way that ensures affected communities have sufficient access to appropriate care. Opioid overdoses currently claim the lives of 185 Americans per day. This epidemic is alarming, not just in its effects on the lives of individuals and families, but also on the light it has shined on the disturbing lack of treatment options in many areas. A number of effective treatments are available for opioid use disorder, but barriers to entry may exist. Aims of the Study: We examine approaches to recruit and encourage providers to undergo workforce training to help address the opioid overdose epidemic. Methods: We conducted a stateâ€wide experiment of nudges and incentives to recruit providers to a learning collaborative on medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in North Carolina. We designed the experiment as a twoâ€stage factorial trial. In the first stage, we randomized 15,835 eligible primary care providers across the state to one of four recruitment arms in a crossâ€cutting design. Providers were first randomized to either a ''proâ€social nudges'' messaging arm, in which recruitment materials incorporated specific information on the opioid epidemic in a provider's community, or to a standard recruitment approach which did not include proâ€social language. Orthogonally crossing these two arms, we further randomized providers to a ''financial incentive'' messaging arm indicating that financial reimbursement for participation was available or to an arm that omitted mention of any financial support for participation. In the second stage of the experiment, recruited providers (n=72) were randomized into one of three levels of performance pay tied to participation in learning collaborative sessions. This experimental design allowed us to estimate the effects of each combination of recruitment nudge and performance pay and, importantly, to separate the selection effects of different recruitment nudges from the incentive effects of performance pay. Results: We highlight several main findings. First, we find that prosocial messaging combined with mention of financial reimbursement yielded a significantly higher number of responses than the control group, while each nudge was ineffective in isolation. Second, there was substantial heterogeneity in provider response by type: nurse practitioners were substantially more likely to respond than other types of primary care providers. Third, recruited providers offered performance pay participated in significantly more sessions, with participation approximately linearly increasing in reimbursement size. Discussion: We use our experimental results to analyze how recruitment nudges and partitionâ€based incentives can be optimized to costâ€effectively recruit and train providers to address the opioid crisis. Beyond this, our results contribute to several strands of academic literature in health, labor, and behavioral economics. Implications for Health Policies: These recruitment methods could be implemented in a lowâ€cost manner for other regions to enhance the provider workforce.

In partnership with a large Medicare Advantage (MA) insurer (Humana, Inc.) and as part of a Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation demonstration program of Valueâ€Based Insurance Design (VBID), the investigators propose to study a randomized controlled quality improvement trial in which Humana randomized MA beneficiaries with COPD to receive proactive outreach for a VBID benefit that provided large reductions in costâ€sharing for their maintenance inhalers and telephoneâ€based COPD medication management services in 2020 and 2021. The investigators will analyze changes in racial disparities for inhaler fills, clinical outcomes, health care spending, and acute care utilization.

Objectives: The current packaging for a 30â€day supply of lenvatinib is based on daily dose and requires that new 30â€day packs be dispensed for most dose reductions. We sought to quantify the expected annual overspending due to current packaging associated with lenvatinib dose reductions in patients with advanced or recurrent microsatellite stable/mismatch repair proficient (MSS/pMMR) endometrial cancer in the United States. Methods: Based on the KEYNOTEâ€775/Study 209 randomized controlled trial, which led to FDA approval of lenvatinib/pembrolizumab for patients with recurrent MSS endometrial cancer after platinum therapy, we constructed a decision model in TreeAge Pro Healthcare 2020 to estimate the annual overspending due to dose reductions during a treatment period of six months. We assumed a starting daily dose of 20mg, with patients requiring dose reductions based on the KEYNOTEâ€775/Study 309. All dose reductions required a new dose pack, except a dose reduction from 18mg to 14mg. We estimated the cost of six months of treatment if alternative packaging or a noâ€cost pill exchange program were offered. Overspending was calculated as the difference between the two 6â€month estimates. An alternative scenario assuming a starting dose of 18mg or 14mg was also modeled based on clinical relevance. Model parameters are detailed in Table 1. Results: The cost of a 30â€day dose pack of lenvatinib is $23,624.40 per patient, irrespective of the daily dose. Based on our assumptions, approximately 7,985 endometrial cancer patients annually in the US will be eligible to receive lenvatinib. Assuming a 20mg starting dose and accounting for expected dose reductions, the 6â€month cost of lenvatinib for this population is estimated to be $1,312,760,659. If a starter pack or a noâ€cost pill exchange were offered, the 6â€month cost of lenvatinib for this population would be $1,131,845,004. Overspending due to the current dose packaging is estimated to be $180,915,655. An alternative scenario assuming an 18mg or 14mg starting dose would reduce the estimated overspending to $46,941,682. Conclusions: The current packaging of lenvatinib is estimated to result in $46.9â€180.9 million of annual overspending that is avoidable through different packaging. A noâ€cost pill exchange program or alternative packaging that is not amenable to dose reductions should be introduced by manufacturers of oral antineoplastic drugs.[Formula presented]

Healthcare systems in the United States (U.S.) have long faced the considerable challenge of managing budgetary pressures while at the same time helping people with serious mental illness and/or addiction. One potential way to address this challenge is to offer communityâ€based services for individuals who are highâ€utilizers of expensive emergency and inpatient psychiatric services. Due to the decentralized nature of California governance, responsibility for mental health services falls primarily to the individual counties. The County of Santa Clara, CA invests significantly in communityâ€based services as well as 24â€hour care settings. This County adopted an innovative Pay for Performance (PFP) model and contracted with a new care provider to better meet the needs of this patient population and, in turn, reduce demand on the County's 24â€hour psychiatric services. Whether this innovative contracting framework will help individuals who thus far have not responded well to mental health services is unknown. The purpose of this study was to determine whether the quality of care for these highâ€need patients was improved and at a sustainable cost. To this end, a randomized clinical trial (RCT) was conducted to determine whether this innovative quality improvement initiative, referred to as "Partners in Wellness", was successful at reducing the total cost of 24â€hour psychiatric care used by enrollees compared to individuals who concurrently received services from the county. Individuals were randomly assigned to the Usual Care (UC) or Payâ€Forâ€Performance (PFP) conditions. The primary outcome of this evaluation was reduction in the total cost of 24â€hour psychiatric services in the target population. the primary outcome of this evaluation was reduction in the total cost of 24â€hour psychiatric services in the target population.

BACKGROUND: Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCIâ€A) is the most recent bundled payment program from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). Under BPCIâ€A, hospitals and physician group providers (PGPs) elect to participate in any of 32 clinical episodes across 8 service lines, where they assume accountability for the costs and quality of care across a hospital admission and 90 days post discharge. The highest volume surgical bundle is lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR). Past studies have evaluated prior bundled payment programs for LEJR, finding modest reductions in spending with no change in quality. However, no studies have examined the effects of participation in LEJR episodes in BPCIâ€A or compared outcomes for hospitals to PGPs. Our objective was to compare the effect of BPCIâ€A on healthcare spending and quality for hospitals and PGPs participating in BPCIâ€A LEJR episodes. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients receiving LEJR using Medicare claims data from 2016â€2018 Q3 (preâ€BPCIâ€A) and 2018 Q4â€2019 Q3 (BPCIâ€A Model Years 1 and 2). We identified hospitals and PGPs participating in BPCIâ€A for LEJR episodes. We used propensity score matching to identify a comparison group of hospitals and PGPs that did not participate in any episode included in the orthopedic service line for BPCIâ€A. We conducted a differenceâ€inâ€differences analysis comparing patients receiving care from LEJR participants versus matched nonâ€participants. This quasiexperimental design mirrored a 2x2 factorial randomized trial in which patients received care from either PGPs in BPCIâ€A for LEJR, hospitals in BPCIâ€A for LEJR, both, or neither. Our primary outcome was 90â€day total episode spending. Secondary outcomes included 30â€day spending and 30â€ and 90â€day mortality and readmissions. RESULTS: PGP participants in BPCIâ€A for LEJR had lower spending than PGP nonâ€participants at 90 days (adjusted differenceâ€inâ€difference [aDID] â€$657, 95% CI â€$792, â€$522, p<0.001). Hospital participants had no significant difference in spending compared to nonâ€participants at 90 days. At 30 days, spending was significantly lower for both PGP and hospital participants than for respective nonâ€participants (PGP aDID â€$515, 95% CI â€$611, â€$421, p<0.001; hospital aDID â€$301, 95% CI â€$466, â€$137, p<0.001). Compared to LEJR BPCIâ€A episodes at hospitals, episodes at PGPs saved $455 more at 90 days (95% CI $213, $698, p<0.001) and $214 more at 30 days (95% CI $44, $385, p=0.01). There were no significant differences in readmissions or mortality for either participant type at 30 or 90 days. CONCLUSIONS: We find that PGPs participating in LEJR episodes in BPCIâ€A had significantly lower spending compared to BPCIâ€A participating hospitals without changes in mortality or readmissions for either participant type. Future bundled payment models should consider the different potential for cost savings across participant types to optimize impact on cost and quality.

Purpose : Performing ptosis surgery in an officeâ€based setting is less costly to the health system relative to an operating room. However, 90% of US ptosis surgeries are performed in operating rooms. This study aims to understand the financial and practical factors involved in surgical location decisionâ€making, and the modifiable incentives to influence migration from operating to procedure room. Methods : Oculoplastic surgeons were surveyed to determine key attributes when deciding to perform a surgery in an operating room (OR) or office procedure room (PR). Responses were collated and common themes extracted. Consensus themes were operationalized into major domains: reimbursement, comorbidities, sedation requirements, and logistics. In a subsequent survey, reimbursement consisted of five levels starting at $550, with each level increasing by 50%, until total reimbursement tripled at $1650. Comorbidities, sedation requirements, and logistics each had two levels, with one being preferable. A discrete choice analysis was used to evaluate each factor's impact. Participants were randomly assigned 14/40 hypothetical ptosis procedure scenarios, choosing between OR/PR. For all scenarios, OR reimbursement was $550. Physician characteristics were collected: urban/rural location, surgeryâ€center ownership, age/experience, and annual number of ptosis surgeries performed. Results : 73 oculoplastic surgeons completed the survey, yielding 1022 observations. Increasing PR reimbursement increased probability of choosing PR, with diminishing effects above $1100. Serious comorbidities/sedationâ€requirements/logistical issues reduced the probability of PR choice, while rural offices and annual number of surgeries increased the probability. Ownership and years of experience were not significant. Conclusions : The model revealed reimbursement is the most important factor, especially at $1100 or more, followed by practice location, sedation, comorbidities, logistical issues and number of surgeries. The results suggest if all risk factors are low, doubling reimbursement increases the likelihood of using the PR by 35% (from 28% to 63%). If all risk factors are high, the likelihood increases by 17% (from 6% to 23%). This study shed light on factors informing ptosis surgery location choice and insights gained will likely inform policy decisions, leading to better allocation of resources.

The investigators will follow probabilityâ€based cohorts of adult nonâ€medical marijuanausers (N=1,500; ages 21+) and susceptible adolescents and young adults (AYA) users(N=1,000; ages 15â€20) over four years. The investigators will use a prospective survey tocollect marijuana use information and will conduct volumetric choice experiments (VCEs)where participants choose quantities to purchase among three legal product prototypes:flower, edible, and concentrate; and one illegal flower product, under simulated retailmarijuana tax structures. The presentation of edibles and concentrates will change overtime to capture the range of product varieties in the market and to accommodate newproducts and characteristics as they evolve. Choice experiments including VCEs use aseries of manipulations as a measurement device to elicit preferences for products andconsumption. Therefore, the experimental design is withinâ€subjects with repeatedmeasures, which allow for causal identifications of the impact of design attributes(e.g., tax bases and rates) on preference and consumption outcomes. The attributes andlevels are selected to reflect THC levels in the market, existing (weight, price, tieredprice by forms) and novel (potency) tax bases, existing (10%â€40% of retail price orequivalent in other bases) and potential (high 60% and 80% of retail prices orequivalent) tax rates, and price distribution for each product. Price distribution levels(5 to 95 percentiles) will come from our price data collection and will be updated overtime and vary by participants' state and locality of residence.Before the experiment, study personnel will instruct participants 1) how to answer thechoice experiment question, including considering their weekly expenditures whenanswering VCE questions; 2) that there is no access to other products, no stockpiling, noselling or giving away products to others, etc., to ensure that participants chooseproducts that reflect their usual purchase patterns for selfâ€use; 3) that there are noright or wrong responses. Study personnel will instruct participants to answer allquestions honestly, thoughtfully, and to the best of their understanding as if they wereactually in this situation, to reduce hypothetical bias; 4) that there may be potentialcosts or issues associated with purchasing illegal products, including risks ofpenalties, undefined potency, possible contamination, and inconsistent product quality;and 5) that participants should keep their weekly budget in mind when making purchasechoices of the products. In VCEs, the investigators will manipulate THC levels, tax ratesand bases, and price levels. Participants will be asked to answer the following: "Imaginethese are the marijuana products that you (participants) can purchase for nonâ€medicaluse, how many of each product would you (participants) most likely buy next time?"Participants can choose more than one product, and as they choose quantities, the totalbalance will be displayed. To make the tasks easier, study personnel will 1) set awarning to inform participants if their reported budget exceeds their weekly budget forspending; 2) provide a dropdown list for quantities or, if they would like more unitsthan the listed, they can fill in a number; and 3) all products are described ashighâ€quality to allow for a comparison of prices. Half of the participants will berandomized to see itemized preâ€tax tag price, excise taxes, and sales taxes, as requestedin some states (e.g., Illinois); the other half will be randomized to see only pricesthat are inclusive of excise taxes. This will allow us to whether excise taxes are moreeffective when applied at checkout compared to hidden in the tag prices.
